In a river town five hundred years ago, every household boils its well water each morning with a pinch of dried bitter herb, explaining to its children that the bitter smell drives away river ghosts that cause summer fever. The households that keep the custom stay well through August, while travelers who drink straight from the well fall sick.

Did the practice work? Yes: boiling killed the waterborne bacteria before anyone drank them. Does the healthy town prove that river ghosts flee from bitter herbs? No. A foolish modern reformer who visits the town, proves that river ghosts do not exist, and therefore tells the families to stop boiling their water will bring summer fever back within a season. An equally foolish traditionalist who insists that because the town stayed healthy, every word of the ghost account is literal truth prevents the town from ever learning bacteriology. The boiling was justified by the health of the town; the ghost account was not. Later testing justified a different explanation: heat destroys microscopic pathogens in contaminated water, with or without the herb. **Reality judges consequences and practices directly; the explanation attached to a working practice must be tested on its own evidence.**

alternates.label: real-life only: China & England boiled water for tea (Gordon 1884 verified)
alternates.text:
For centuries in China, households kept the custom of boiling their drinking water to steep tea rather than drinking raw well or canal water, explaining through traditional medical theory that raw water carried cold and dampness that harmed the stomach. Medical officers reporting from Peking and Shanghai in the 1870s recorded that the Chinese drank boiled water almost exclusively and escaped much of the waterborne cholera and dysentery common in crowded cities (C. A. Gordon, *Epitome of the Reports of the Medical Officers to the Chinese Imperial Maritime Customs Service*, 1884). A parish-level study of eighteenth-century England found the same pattern: as tea drinking spread, mortality fell sharply in parishes with poorer water quality long before anyone understood bacteria (Francisca Antman, *Review of Economics and Statistics*, 2023).

Did the practice work? Yes: boiling killed waterborne bacteria before anyone drank them. Does the lower death rate prove that raw water injures the body through cold and dampness? No. A foolish modern reformer who disproves the traditional balance theory and therefore tells households to stop boiling their water brings cholera and dysentery back within a season. An equally foolish traditionalist who insists that because the custom saved lives, every word of the pre-modern explanation is literal truth prevents medicine from ever learning bacteriology. The boiling was justified by the lower death rate; the balance theory was not. Later testing, culminating in Robert Koch's isolation of the cholera bacillus in 1883, justified a different explanation: heat destroys microscopic pathogens in contaminated water, with or without the tea leaves. **Reality judges consequences and practices directly; the explanation attached to a working practice must be tested on its own evidence.**

alternates.label: real-life only: Mesoamerican nixtamalization & U.S. pellagra epidemic
alternates.text:
For centuries across Mesoamerica, farming peoples boiled and soaked dried maize in water mixed with wood ash or slaked lime before grinding it into dough, treating the step as an inherited culinary custom without any knowledge of vitamin chemistry. Populations living chiefly on maize prepared that way remained free of pellagra. When European settlers and later farmers in the American South adopted maize as a cheap staple crop while discarding the traditional lime-soaking custom, pellagra swept across corn-dependent counties, killing tens of thousands of Americans in the early twentieth century.

Did the practice work? Yes: the alkaline bath broke open the hull and freed bound niacin so the human digestive tract could absorb it. Does the healthy population prove that every traditional account attached to the kitchen custom was literal biochemistry? No. An impatient reformer who discards a working custom because its practitioners cannot give a modern scientific explanation invites catastrophe; a traditionalist who refuses controlled testing never learns why the custom worked. In 1914 and 1915, Dr. Joseph Goldberger of the U.S. Public Health Service proved through dietary trials that pellagra was a nutritional deficiency rather than an infection, and in 1937 Conrad Elvehjem isolated niacin as the missing nutrient. **Reality judges consequences and practices directly; the explanation attached to a working practice must be tested on its own evidence.**

items.quote:
A port authority administers the same **Harbor Pilot's Examination** on tides, shoals, and channel charts to a hundred candidates. Every candidate had access to the same charts, the same training cruises, and the same two hours in a quiet room. The examinations are graded anonymously by candidate number so the board cannot see any candidate's name, race, sex, or family background.

One candidate spent twelve hours a week all year studying currents and soundings and has a sharp grasp of seamanship; he scores **98 out of 100**. Another spent two hours a week studying and struggles to read a tidal chart; he scores **54 out of 100**.

**The examination was not unjust because the two candidates received unequal scores.** The unequal outcome is the **truthful measurement** of different preparation and competence under an identical procedure.

If the port commissioner intervenes, declares the unequal scores proof of systemic injustice, discards the examination, and grants both men the same harbor pilot's license, two failures occur at once: first, the port confiscates the reward of diligent labor and teaches the next class of apprentices that study is pointless; second, **it falsifies reality** and puts an incompetent pilot onto the deck of a forty-thousand-ton ship entering a rocky channel.
items.problem: Follow-up on research hold 71f5446f (looking for a real-life case where discarding objective exams collided with physical/operational reality rather than ending only in a court judgment): Two totalitarian states actually abolished individual entrance and engineering exams to equalize class outcomes and were forced by industrial reality to restore them: (1) the Soviet Union (1928-1932 class quotas and collective 'brigade' grading, abolished by the Central Executive Committee decree of September 19, 1932 because newly graduated engineers lacked the mathematics and physics to run industrial plants), and (2) China's Cultural Revolution (1966-1977 abolition of the gaokao, reversed under Deng Xiaoping in 1977, who compared examinations to factory quality control). Alternate (c) offers the U.S. FAA's 2014 biographical questionnaire, which worsened controller staffing shortages until Congress barred it in Public Law 114-190, Section 2106 (verified in ext-ref/faa/PLAW-114publ190.htm). Note: Soviet 1932 decree and Deng 1977 primary texts are not yet saved locally in ext-ref/.

Twentieth-century history tested that error at national scale twice, and physical reality forced both regimes to reverse course. During the First Five-Year Plan (1928 to 1932), the Soviet Union bypassed individual entrance examinations in technical institutes to fill engineering seats by class quotas and graded students collectively in brigades; when graduates proved unable to keep industrial plants running, the Central Executive Committee issued its decree of September 19, 1932 abolishing collective grading and restoring individual examinations and theses. China repeated the experiment during the Cultural Revolution, abolishing the national university entrance examination (*gaokao*) in 1966 in favor of class-background recommendations; eleven years of crippled technical training forced Deng Xiaoping to restore the examination in 1977, stating that examinations check students' work just as the testing of factory products checks industrial quality.

alternates.label: replace with Soviet 1932 & China 1977 engineering-exam reversals
alternates.text:
Twentieth-century history ran this experiment at national scale twice, and physical reality overruled ideology in both cases. During the First Five-Year Plan (1928 to 1932), the Soviet state bypassed individual entrance examinations in technical institutes to fill engineering seats by class origin and graded students collectively in permanent brigades rather than as individuals. Graduates who lacked basic mathematics and physics could not keep complex factories operating, forcing the Central Executive Committee on September 19, 1932 to abolish collective brigade grading and restore strict individual examinations and graduation theses.

China repeated the same experiment during the Cultural Revolution. In 1966 the government abolished the national university entrance examination (*gaokao*) on the ground that anonymous academic testing favored the privileged and produced unequal outcomes across classes, admitting students from 1970 to 1976 by political reliability and class-background recommendation instead.

**Abolishing objective examinations did not equalize technical competence.** It left factories, hospitals, and research institutes short of trained engineers and scientists while teaching an entire generation that disciplined study counted for less than political pedigree. In 1977 Deng Xiaoping ordered the immediate restoration of the national merit examination, telling China's science and education leaders that examinations check students' mastery just as the testing of factory products serves as quality control. Even a state with absolute political power cannot decree around physical competence.

A modern regulatory example occurred in American aviation. In 2014 the Federal Aviation Administration replaced its skills-based air traffic controller screening pipeline with a biographical questionnaire aimed at broadening demographic outcomes, disqualifying trained aviation graduates and worsening controller staffing bottlenecks across the airspace system. Two years later, Congress intervened in the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (Public Law 114-190, Section 2106), prohibiting the agency from using biographical assessments for experienced and targeted controller pools and directing it to reconsider disqualified applicants.

items.quote:
#### The Hill Town Grain Storehouse and the Rats: Why False Compassion Harms the Weakest First

Even when the person advocating "compassion over rules" is not a calculating Marcusean strategist, but merely a sentimental citizen who dislikes seeing anyone punished, the following case illustrates who actually bears the cost when a community adopts the Compassionate Delusion:

> **The Hill Town Grain Storehouse and the Rats:** In a stone town on a hill, fifty families store their winter barley in a row of bins inside the municipal storehouse. At one end of the building stand the thick, iron-lined stone bins of the wealthy grain merchant; at the other end stand the thin pine-plank bins of the elderly widows and day-laborers, holding just enough barley to keep them alive until April.
>
> In November, rats tunnel under the storehouse wall. The town watchman sets heavy iron traps along the floorboards. The next morning, a sentimental committee visits the storehouse, sees three dead rats in the traps, and protests that the creatures were merely hungry, that the traps are cruel, and that a compassionate town must prohibit all traps, poison, and terriers.
>
> The town council yields to the sentimentalists and prohibits all rat control. The sentimentalists congratulate themselves at every social gathering on their humanity.
>
> **In January, the condition of the storehouse reveals the consequence.** Prohibiting the traps did not stop the rats from feeding; it only decided whose barley they consumed. Their teeth could not penetrate the wealthy merchant's iron-lined stone bins, and even if he lost ten percent of his grain, his family still had ample food for the winter. Instead, the rats gnawed straight through the thin pine boards of the poor widows' and laborers' bins, consumed their winter grain, and fouled what remained.
>
> By February, the poor widows are starving in the cold, while the sentimentalists who prohibited the traps sit in their warm parlors praising their own "empathy."

The operational principle in that storehouse applies across society: When a society refuses to restrain criminals, thieves, rioters, and disorderly students in the name of "compassion," the wealthy can always purchase high walls, gated communities, private security guards, and private tutors. It is the law-abiding working-class family, the elderly widow on public transit, and the capable poor child sitting in a disordered public classroom whose thin pine bins are destroyed. Enforcing order, standards, and law is the truest compassion a city can show to its industrious poor.
items.problem: Follow-up on research hold 561a100e ('Unless there is a clearer example, perhaps let's keep a version of the fictional account'): Checked Philadelphia's 2012-13 suspension ban (Lacoe & Steinberg 2018) and Oregon Measure 110 (2020-2024); modern policy studies carry confounders that blunt the clean mechanism. Meanwhile, The Hill Town Grain Storehouse and the Rats is now the sole grain-storehouse fable left in the entire book (since Ch 2, Ch 6, Ch 9, and Ch 10 all moved off grain/storehouses), and it lands every beat directly. Alternate (a) keeps the fable verbatim and adds one tight sentence from verified BJS data (ext-ref/bjs/hpnvv0812.pdf); Ignore keeps the fable completely untouched.
